VIP Ireland
  A full website built from scratch for VIP Ireland, an Irish distributor of professional aesthetic machines and advanced EMS devices.
  ← Projects



  





  About the project
  VIP Ireland is an Irish distributor for a range of professional aesthetic machines and advanced EMS devices, catering to clinics, therapists, and wellness businesses across Ireland. The client needed a clean, credible website that communicated the premium nature of the product range and made it easy for potential partners to get in touch.
  This was my first website built entirely from scratch using WordPress and Elementor Pro. I handled everything from the initial setup and theme configuration through to page design, navigation structure, content layout, and mobile responsiveness.





  What I built
  
    
      Pages
      VIP Hi-Line, Modules, FAQ, About us, Become a partner, Contact
    
    
      Tools used
      WordPress, Elementor Pro, custom CSS
    
    
      Focus areas
      Layout design, branding, mobile responsiveness, navigation structure
    
    
      Outcome
      Fully live professional website at vipireland.ie
    
  





  Reflection
  As my first WordPress project, VIP Ireland was a steep but rewarding learning curve. Getting to grips with Elementor Pro, understanding how WordPress themes and plugins interact, and learning to build responsive layouts took time and iteration. By the end of the project I had a solid foundation in the platform and a finished site I was genuinely proud of.
  The experience taught me how to translate a client brief into a real working product, manage the full build process independently, and deliver something polished on a live domain.

title: PriceBeo
text:
About the project
PriceBeo is a mobile app that lets users scan any product barcode in-store and instantly compare prices across Ireland’s five major retailers: Tesco, Dunnes Stores, Lidl, Aldi and SuperValu. With grocery prices up 27% since 20211 and limited tools available to Irish shoppers, the app targets a clear and validated market gap.
As CTO, my role was to lead the technical vision and strategy for the platform, translate between the business team and technical advisors, and make informed architecture decisions. I contributed the analytical spine with input from the team across the sections below. The group then built that analysis into the investor-ready report and pitch deck.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The sections below reproduce the core analytics from the PriceBeo business plan as executable Python with Plotly. The original pitch used static exhibits; this page rebuilds the same underlying model interactively for the portfolio. Every chart is generated live from the numbers in the business report. Click the </> Code button at the top of the page to toggle all source code, or unfold any single chunk to inspect it.

1. Market context: concentrated by design
Ireland’s grocery market is worth approximately €13 billion a year and is highly concentrated. The top five retailers capture 92.3% of spend, leaving 7.7% for everyone else2. Any price comparison tool that wants to cover Irish shoppers meaningfully needs to cover these five, which is exactly what PriceBeo does.

TipWhy this matters commercially



The 89% download intent is the single most important number in the plan. It converts an abstract market opportunity (€13 billion, five retailers) into a specific addressable population. Applied to Ireland’s 2.1 million grocery households, even heavily discounted real-world conversion rates produce a credible path to the 15,000 year-one MAU target.

3. The revenue model
PriceBeo runs a freemium model. The app is free to download. A €2.99 per month Premium tier unlocks basket comparison, price alerts, back-in-stock alerts and personalised savings reports. Revenue comes from three streams: Premium subscriptions, in-app advertising and retailer affiliate income. The business carries a 92% gross margin throughout the three-year plan because variable costs are limited to server, API and payment-processing fees.

title: PriceBeo
text:
5. Unit economics
The financial projections live or die on unit economics. For a freemium SaaS-style business the core question is not “how much revenue”, it is whether each acquired Premium user generates enough lifetime value to cover acquisition cost.






NoteThe two numbers that matter



Customer acquisition cost (CAC): €1.31. Calculated from total Year 1 marketing spend (€19,700) divided by acquired users (15,000 MAU).
Lifetime value (LTV): depends on retention. Industry consumer-app benchmarks suggest 12 to 24 months typical retention for a freemium utility with weekly use cases. PriceBeo’s weekly shop cadence places it at the high end.


The calculation below is an extension I built for this portfolio to stress-test the LTV assumption across three retention scenarios. The €1.31 CAC and 92% gross margin come from the original financial model; the sensitivity analysis itself was not in the pitch but is a natural follow-on to the numbers the model produces.


Code
import pandas as pd

price_per_month  = 2.99
gross_margin     = 0.92
cac              = 1.31
retention_scenarios = {"Conservative (12 mo)": 12, "Base case (18 mo)": 18, "Optimistic (24 mo)": 24}

rows = []
for name, months_retained in retention_scenarios.items():
    ltv = price_per_month * months_retained * gross_margin
    rows.append({
        "Scenario": name,
        "Retention (months)": months_retained,
        "LTV (€)": round(ltv, 2),
        "LTV:CAC ratio": f"{ltv / cac:.1f}x",
        "Months to recover CAC": round(cac / (price_per_month * gross_margin), 2),
    })

economics = pd.DataFrame(rows)

A LTV:CAC ratio above 3x is considered healthy for consumer SaaS. PriceBeo’s base case sits at 38x. Even under the conservative 12-month retention scenario, the ratio is 25x. The business recovers CAC in 0.48 months, well under two weeks.

8. Technical architecture
As CTO my core contribution was validating that the technical model was feasible at the price point the financials required. PriceBeo runs on a stateless REST API fronting a PostgreSQL database that holds the barcode-indexed product catalogue and retailer price feeds. Scans run through Google ML Kit on-device, which avoids round-trip latency and keeps the scan-to-result time under two seconds.

title: PriceBeo
text:
Reflection
PriceBeo was the most demanding and rewarding project of my degree. Working across four assignments over the full academic year, the project developed my ability to think like a founder: validating a real problem, designing a technically sound solution, building a financial model that survives scrutiny and pitching to investors under time pressure.
The most valuable lesson was learning to hold technical decisions and commercial realities in tension at the same time. As CTO I repeatedly had to choose between technically cleaner architectures and commercially sensible ones. The PostgreSQL decision is a good example: a NoSQL document store would have been faster to build, but PostgreSQL’s strict schema gave the data accuracy guarantees the consumer trust narrative depended on. That kind of trade-off does not exist in a module exercise with a single optimisation target. It only emerges when technical, financial and brand decisions sit in the same meeting.
Building the analytical sections on this page was a separate exercise from the module itself. The original pitch used static exhibits in a PowerPoint deck; reproducing the same underlying model as executable Python with Plotly for this portfolio forced me to revisit every assumption end-to-end. A 10-year diagnostic and predictive analytics engagement on EcoEnergy Corp, a global sustainable infrastructure and technology company operating across five continents. The team’s brief was to identify the drivers of the company’s €8.46M net loss and recommend a restructuring path back to profitability. title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
text:
About the project
EcoEnergy Corp is a global sustainable infrastructure and technology company selling across three categories (Technology, Construction, Transport & Insurance) in five regions. The dataset covered 10 years of sales, costs, channels and discount rates with sufficient granularity to support both regional diagnostics and product-level recommendations.
Group 4 was structured as a regional consulting team. Each member led the analysis for one region: I covered Asia, with the other four regions allocated to Niall Grainger (North America), Roisin Murphy (Europe), Daniel Vala (Africa) and Martinas Jucys-Brady (South America). The cross-regional synthesis (outsourcing strategy, predictive forecast, industry benchmarking) was developed collectively. This page reproduces the team’s collective findings, with the Asia section reflecting analysis I led directly.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The visualisations below reproduce the core findings from our Power BI consulting deliverable as interactive Plotly charts. The original deliverable was a multi-page Power BI report with a star-schema data model, DAX KPIs, drill-through navigation and a forecasting layer. This page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as executable Python with Plotly for the portfolio. All numerical results originate from the dataset and Power BI report submitted for assessment.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
text:
1. The portfolio is failing
Before any regional or product analysis, the topline numbers established the scale of the problem. EcoEnergy generated €130.7M in revenue across the 10-year window but incurred €139.1M in costs, producing a €8.46M cumulative net loss. The portfolio breakdown is more revealing than the top line: 39% of all products were sold at a loss, and 8 of the 10 product lines were collectively unprofitable across the period.


Code
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

portfolio = pd.DataFrame({
    "Status":   ["Sold at a profit", "Sold at a loss"],
    "Share":    [60.6, 39.4],
    "Detail":   ["Insurance plans, solar panels and Construction lines in Europe drove the bulk of profitable activity",
                 "Smartphones, tablets, printers, cars and persistent loss-makers across regions"],
})

fig = go.Figure(go.Pie(
    labels=portfolio["Status"],
    values=portfolio["Share"],
    hole=0.55,
    marker=dict(colors=["#1e7e34", "#c8102e"], line=dict(color="white", width=2)),
    textinfo="label+percent",
    textposition="outside",
    sort=False,
    hovertemplate="<b>%{label}</b><br>%{percent}<br>%{customdata}<extra></extra>",
    customdata=portfolio["Detail"],
))

fig.add_annotation(
    text="<b>€8.46M</b><br>net loss<br>10-year cumulative",
    x=0.5, y=0.5, showarrow=False,
    font=dict(size=14, color="#1a1a1a"),
)

fig.update_layout(
    height=440,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=20, b=20),
    showlegend=False,
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Portfolio profitability split: 39% of all units sold made a loss, 61% made a profit. The €8.46M net loss is the integrated effect of a small profitable cohort being insufficient to offset a much larger loss-making cohort.




The interpretation that matters analytically is that the loss is not a market problem (revenue exists) but a portfolio composition and cost discipline problem. That framing shaped every subsequent diagnostic decision: the question was not “how do we sell more”, it was “which products and regions should we keep, drop, or restructure”.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
text:
2. Regional performance scorecard
Aggregating to the regional level surfaces five distinct patterns. North America’s losses were the largest in absolute terms but the cause (sub-cost pricing on key product lines) was clear. Africa was loss-making with high cost as the structural driver. Europe was profitable in some categories but volatile. South America was a low-cost manufacturing leader but with weak Insurance and Transport performance. Asia is the case I analysed most closely, and the finding there is the one I want to spend most time on.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

regions = pd.DataFrame({
    "Region":    ["North America", "Africa", "South America", "Europe", "Asia"],
    "Revenue":   [29.5, 25.17, 25.35, 26.6, 24.05],
    "NetProfit": [-4.15, -3.7, -0.61, -0.14, 0.14],
    "Driver":    ["Sub-cost pricing on key tech and transport lines",
                  "Structural cost disadvantage in Technology",
                  "Low manufacturing costs but weak Transport / Insurance",
                  "Profitable in Construction; volatile elsewhere",
                  "High revenue masked by aggressive discounting"],
})

regions = regions.sort_values("NetProfit", ascending=True)

fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2,
                    subplot_titles=("Revenue (€ millions)", "Net profit / loss (€ millions)"),
                    horizontal_spacing=0.18)

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    y=regions["Region"], x=regions["Revenue"],
    orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color="#4a90a4"),
    text=[f"€{v:.1f}M" for v in regions["Revenue"]],
    textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(size=11),
    showlegend=False,
), row=1, col=1)

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    y=regions["Region"], x=regions["NetProfit"],
    orientation="h",
    marker=dict(color=["#c8102e" if v < 0 else "#1e7e34" for v in regions["NetProfit"]]),
    text=[f"€{v:+.2f}M" for v in regions["NetProfit"]],
    textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(size=11),
    showlegend=False,

Figure 2: Regional revenue and net profit/loss across the 10-year window. Asia generated the highest revenue but near-zero net profit; North America was the largest absolute loss-maker; Africa’s losses were structural rather than cyclical.




Worth stating plainly: only Asia ended the 10-year window in marginal profit, and it did so on the back of a single recovery year (2024) after six years of losses. The other four regions were all negative. This is what “8 of 10 products unprofitable” looks like when you decompose it geographically.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
section: 3. Asia deep-dive: revenue is not profit
text:
3. Asia deep-dive: revenue is not profit
This was my regional analysis. Asia generated €24.05M in revenue across the decade, the highest of any region, but produced only €0.14M in net profit. That is a 0.6% margin on the most active geography in the portfolio. The diagnostic question was why such strong topline activity translated into almost no margin.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go

asia_years = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year":   list(range(2015, 2025)),
    "Profit": [0.42, 0.51, 0.38, -0.18, -0.31, -0.42, -0.55, -0.48, -0.36, 1.13],
    "Phase":  ["Profitable", "Profitable", "Profitable",
               "Loss-making", "Loss-making", "Loss-making", "Loss-making", "Loss-making", "Loss-making",
               "Recovery"],
})

phase_colours = {"Profitable": "#1e7e34", "Loss-making": "#c8102e", "Recovery": "#d4a017"}

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=asia_years["Year"], y=asia_years["Profit"],
    marker=dict(color=[phase_colours[p] for p in asia_years["Phase"]]),
    text=[f"€{v:+.2f}M" for v in asia_years["Profit"]],
    textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(size=10),
    showlegend=False,
    hovertemplate="<b>%{x}</b><br>Profit: €%{y:.2f}M<br>Phase: %{customdata}<extra></extra>",
    customdata=asia_years["Phase"],
))

fig.add_hline(y=0, line=dict(color="#1a1a1a", width=1.5))

for phase, colour in phase_colours.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=[None], y=[None],
        marker=dict(color=colour),
        name=phase, showlegend=True,
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    height=420,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=20, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False, dtick=1),
    yaxis=dict(title="Net profit / loss (€ millions)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", range=[-0.8, 1.5]),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 3: Asia 10-year profit pattern. Three distinct phases: an early profitable period (2015 to 2017) on disciplined portfolio management, a sustained loss-making period (2018 to 2023) driven by aggressive discounting and persistence with loss-making lines, and a 2024 recovery as the portfolio tightened.




The 2018 to 2023 period coincided with two compounding decisions: aggressive online discounting (Asia’s online channel dominates the regional sales mix) and continued investment in product lines that were structurally unprofitable for the region (flight tickets, insurance, printers, certain tech devices). The 2024 recovery is what happens when those decisions reverse: the team narrowed to the lines where Asia has genuine cost-and-demand fit (cars, solar panels, smartphones, tablets, laptops) and tightened discount discipline.






TipThe Asia lesson generalises



The phrase “high revenue, near-zero profit” is a useful diagnostic flag for any consumer business. It almost always indicates that the discounting structure is funding the volume rather than the margin. The fix is unglamorous: enforce minimum margin thresholds, exit the perennial loss-makers, and accept smaller revenue numbers as the price of real profit. Asia’s 2024 numbers show the trade is worth making.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
text:
4. Where production should actually happen
The team’s central commercial recommendation was an outsourcing strategy based on regional cost advantage at the product level. The “winner-takes-all” sourcing principle (Jain, 2024) directs production to the region with the lowest median unit cost for each product, provided that region has demonstrable cost discipline. Median was preferred over mean to suppress outlier sales records that distorted the production cost picture.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go

cost_data = pd.DataFrame({
    "Region":       ["South America", "Asia",   "Europe",  "North America", "Africa"],
    "Technology":   [339.66,          346.90,   471.20,    458.30,          512.40],
    "Construction": [430.10,          445.50,   511.81,    373.25,          495.80],
    "Transport":    [411.50,          425.30,   380.49,    351.83,          478.20],
})

fig = go.Figure()

categories = {
    "Technology":   "#1e7e34",
    "Construction": "#4a90a4",
    "Transport":    "#d4a017",
}

for category, colour in categories.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        x=cost_data["Region"], y=cost_data[category],
        name=category,
        marker=dict(color=colour),
        text=[f"€{v:.0f}" for v in cost_data[category]],
        textposition="outside",
        textfont=dict(size=10),
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="group",
    height=440,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=20, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False),
    yaxis=dict(title="Median unit cost (€)", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", range=[300, 600]),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Median unit cost by region across the three product categories, 2021 to 2024. South America leads on Technology, Europe leads on demand for Construction (and is the only profitable region in that category), North America leads on absolute Transport unit cost. Africa is the structural cost-disadvantage region across the board.




The recommendation collapses to: Technology → South America and Asia, Construction (building materials) → Europe (because it leads on demand and was the only profitable Construction region), Solar panels → South America (cheapest at €273.42 per unit), Cars and flight tickets → North America, Insurance plans → Europe. Transport and Insurance categories with no defensible regional fit should be exited entirely rather than restructured.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
section: 5. Predictive forecast: from €8.46M loss to €3.09M profit
text:
5. Predictive forecast: from €8.46M loss to €3.09M profit
The predictive layer asked whether the outsourcing recommendation would actually restore profitability if implemented. The forecast applied three conservative adjustments to the cost base: production hub unit costs replaced regional costs, shipping costs were multiplied by 5 to reflect longer-distance logistics from consolidated hubs, and capacity was capped at 50% in Year 1 and 75% in Year 2 to model realistic ramp.


Code
import plotly.graph_objects as go

forecast = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year":     ["Year 1 (50% capacity)", "Year 2 (75% capacity)", "Year 3 (full capacity)"],
    "Revenue":  [3.12, 4.68, 6.22],
    "Profit":   [1.55, 2.32, 3.09],
    "Margin":   [49.7, 49.6, 49.7],
})

fig = go.Figure()

fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=forecast["Year"], y=forecast["Revenue"],
    name="Revenue (€M)",
    marker=dict(color="#4a90a4"),
    text=[f"€{v:.2f}M" for v in forecast["Revenue"]],
    textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(size=11),
))
fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
    x=forecast["Year"], y=forecast["Profit"],
    name="Net profit (€M)",
    marker=dict(color="#1e7e34"),
    text=[f"€{v:.2f}M" for v in forecast["Profit"]],
    textposition="outside",
    textfont=dict(size=11),
))

for i, year in enumerate(forecast["Year"]):
    fig.add_annotation(
        x=year, y=forecast["Revenue"].iloc[i] + 0.5,
        text=f"<b>{forecast['Margin'].iloc[i]:.1f}% margin</b>",
        showarrow=False,
        font=dict(size=11, color="#1a1a1a"),
    )

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="group",
    height=440,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=20, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    xaxis=dict(showgrid=False),
    yaxis=dict(title="€ millions", showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", range=[0, 8]),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Three-year predictive forecast under the outsourcing recommendation. Year 1 returns to modest profit (€1.55M) at 50% capacity, Year 2 expands at 75% capacity, and Year 3 hits a €3.09M annual profit at full capacity (49.7% margin). The reference line is the €8.46M cumulative loss the company is starting from.




Technology accounts for €7.75M of the €15.6M Year 3 revenue forecast, making it the single largest category and the one most sensitive to the outsourcing assumption holding. Construction earns €2M but with weaker margins, raising a follow-on question of whether some Construction lines should also be exited despite Europe’s demand strength. Predictive analytics that produces follow-on diagnostic questions is doing its job; predictive analytics that produces only confidence is usually doing the opposite.

title: EcoEnergy Corp profitability turnaround
text:
Reflection
This was the first project of my degree where the analytical work was the entire point of the deliverable. Strategy projects use frameworks; new enterprise projects use financial models; this was a genuine “make sense of a real dataset and produce a defensible recommendation” engagement. The Power BI deliverable forced a discipline I had not yet developed properly: the figure exists to support the argument, not the other way around. Several of my early Asia drafts had charts that were technically accurate but did not advance the story. Cutting those was harder than producing them.
The Asia finding (highest revenue, near-zero profit) was the moment the dataset taught me something I would not have arrived at by reasoning alone. Going in I had assumed the worst-performing regions would be the obvious laggards on revenue. The truth was the opposite: the region generating the most activity was barely breaking even, because the activity was being subsidised by discounts. That pattern (high revenue masking weak unit economics) is one I now look for in any commercial dataset. I came across it again in a different form during my Machine Learning research paper, where the cost-sensitive threshold work surfaced a similar lesson about apparent performance hiding underlying structural problems.
Working in a five-person consulting team was also instructive. The regional ownership structure (one analyst per continent) gave each member a defensible domain but introduced a real coordination challenge: ensuring the cross-regional synthesis chapters did not contradict the regional ones. We resolved this by having the regional leads peer-review each other’s outsourcing recommendations before they were finalised, which caught two material inconsistencies that would otherwise have shipped. The skills matrix approach we used later in BAA1019 came directly from this engagement.
Rebuilding the Power BI exhibits as Plotly charts for this portfolio was a separate exercise from the module itself. Power BI is the right tool for a recurring corporate dashboard; Plotly is the right tool for a static, narrative-driven portfolio page. Translating between them forced the same discipline as the original analytical work: the figure exists to support the argument, and any chart that does not pass that test should be cut. The final six visualisations on this page are what survived that filter, out of approximately eighteen in the original Power BI report.

title: Future Goals
text:
Career


  
    Short term · 6 to 12 months out
    Business analyst in the gaming industry
    My goal after graduation is a business analyst role in gaming. It is a sector where analytical thinking shapes real product decisions: live-service economies, player retention modelling, monetisation experiments, content release pipelines. The combination of fast-moving product cycles and rich behavioural datasets is exactly the environment I want to operate in early in my career, and the analytical patterns I worked through in my Online Shoppers research paper (cost-sensitive thresholding, threshold-versus-classifier trade-offs) translate directly to the kind of retention and conversion problems gaming analysts work on every day.
  

  
    Location · Late 2026 onward
    Working abroad in London
    London is one of Europe's largest hubs for both gaming and broader analytics work. Relocating after graduation means access to the network, the pace and the role density that early career growth depends on. The intention is to land in London by late 2026 and treat the first twelve months there as deliberately steep: the kind of role where the person sitting next to you knows things you do not, and the gap is the point.

title: Applegreen App Innovation
text:
← Projects

  Project goal
  The assignment required our group to identify a real innovation opportunity for a major Irish enterprise. We chose Applegreen, Ireland's largest fuel and convenience retailer, and focused our research on understanding how the existing customer experience could be improved through technology. Our central argument was that the Applegreen Rewards app, which held a 2-star average on the App Store at the time, was severely undersupplying its users and represented a clear gap in an otherwise strong brand.
  Rather than pitching a vague product idea, we grounded the project in real research. We visited the Applegreen at Blackrock, Co. Dublin, conducted structured customer interviews across multiple days and times, ran a Google survey with 18 respondents, and observed customer behaviour in-store through ethnographic methods. The output was a concrete innovation proposal with a working prototype.





  Research approach
  We identified two core customer segments to anchor our research: pit stoppers, who visit Applegreen primarily in the morning for fuel and food, and hectic commuters, who are price-sensitive, time-pressured, and travel daily from outside Dublin. These two groups accounted for the majority of in-store traffic we observed.
  Our primary research included on-site interviews with customers and the store manager, a Google survey focused on app usage and fuel price transparency, and ethnographic observation by group members who were themselves regular Applegreen customers. Survey results showed that 72.2% of respondents would download or use the app more if it displayed live fuel prices — a clear signal the existing app was missing a high-value feature.





  The innovation proposal
  We proposed transforming the Applegreen Rewards app from a basic loyalty card into a full-service forecourt companion. The core features of our redesign were:
  
    
      01
      
        Live fuel price tracker
        A real-time graph showing current and historical petrol and diesel prices at nearby Applegreen locations, allowing customers to plan when and where to fill up. Given the fuel price volatility in 2022, this feature directly addressed the primary concern of both customer segments.
      
    
    
      02
      
        Click and Collect ordering
        An in-app pre-order system for Braeburn Coffee and deli items, allowing customers to place and pay for orders before arriving at the store. This eliminated queue time for commuters and gave staff advance notice of orders, improving efficiency on both sides.
      
    
    
      03
      
        Apple Wallet and Android Wallet integration
        Adding the Applegreen rewards card to native device wallets so customers could access their card instantly without navigating through a slow app. This removed the single biggest friction point reported in app store reviews.
      
    
    
      04
      
        Full UI overhaul
        A visual redesign to modernise the app's interface, incorporate the Braeburn Coffee brand identity, and create a cleaner, faster experience that encouraged repeat engagement rather than one-off use.
      
    
  





  Skills developed
  
    
      Research
      Primary fieldwork, customer interviews, and survey design
    
    
      Analysis
      Translating survey data into actionable innovation insight
    
    
      Strategy
      Customer segmentation and needs-based product framing
    
    
      Prototyping
      Designing app screen mockups to visualise the solution
    
    
      Collaboration
      Group project coordination across six team members
    
    
      Communication
      Structuring and presenting a business case to a real company
    
  





  Reflection
  This project was one of the first times I worked on a proposal pitched directly to the management of a real company. Knowing that Applegreen's Managing Director, Fiona Matthews, delivered the plenary and would be familiar with the brief made the research feel like it had real stakes. That context pushed the group to treat the fieldwork seriously and ground every recommendation in evidence rather than assumption.
  The most valuable part for me was learning how to connect qualitative insight — things people told us in interviews — with quantitative signal from the survey, and then translate both into a product decision. The 72.2% figure on the live fuel price question was the clearest moment in the project where data directly drove the recommendation, and that kind of evidence-first thinking has shaped how I approach every analysis-based task since.

title: Remote Work and Employee Motivation
text:
← Projects

  Overview
  This assignment was the final submission for SB202 Critical Thinking in Action, worth 25% of the module grade. The brief required me to frame a research question within an established academic field, review relevant peer-reviewed literature, design a primary research methodology, plan a thematic analysis, and consider what the findings might conclude.
  I chose to situate the research in organisational psychology, focusing on employee motivation and satisfaction in remote work environments. The COVID-19 pandemic had accelerated remote work adoption globally, but the long-term effects on motivation and satisfaction remained an open and actively contested area of research — making it a strong candidate for a critical thinking exercise grounded in real academic debate.





  Research question
  What are the key factors influencing employee motivation and satisfaction in remote work environments, and how do these factors differ from traditional office-based work settings?
  The question was designed to sit at the intersection of two well-studied phenomena — the psychology of motivation and the structural shift toward distributed work — so that the literature review could draw on empirical studies from different methodological traditions and the interview design could produce comparable, thematically analysable data.





  Literature reviewed
  
    
      01
      
        Galanti et al. (2021) — Work from home during COVID-19
        This study examined the impact of family-work conflict, social isolation, distracting environments, job autonomy, and self-leadership on productivity, engagement, and stress during the pandemic. It established that remote workers face unique challenges not present in office settings, particularly around balancing family responsibilities and managing isolation, and that these factors directly affect motivation and satisfaction.
      
    
    
      02
      
        Grant, Wallace and Spurgeon (2013) — Psychological factors in remote e-working
        This study explored how remote work affects well-being, job effectiveness, and work-life balance. A key finding was the risk of remote workers becoming "invisible" within organisations — requiring intentional support and recognition structures that do not exist naturally in distributed environments. It highlighted communication, trust-building, and social connection as critical to sustaining motivation when face-to-face interaction is removed.
      
    
    
      03
      
        Gajendran and Harrison (2007) — Telecommuting meta-analysis
        This meta-analysis of psychological mediators and individual consequences found that autonomy, schedule flexibility, and reduced commute stress are the primary satisfaction drivers in remote settings, while office environments derive satisfaction from in-person culture, physical amenities, and social interaction. The study reinforced the need for environment-specific management strategies rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.
      
    
  





  Research design
  The assignment required me to propose a primary research methodology to test the research question empirically. I designed a qualitative interview study with the following parameters:
  
    
      Participant selection
      Cross-industry interviewees with varying lengths of remote work experience, including those who manage remote teams
    
    
      Interview design
      Likert-scale anchored questions on flexibility, with follow-up probes for both positive and negative experiences
    
    
      Analysis method
      Thematic analysis — pre-identified themes from literature coded against transcripts, then compared across demographic groups
    
    
      Key themes
      Work-life balance, autonomy, flexibility, communication barriers, social isolation, and supervisor support
    
  
  The five-step analysis plan moved from pre-interview theme identification through transcript coding, cross-interviewee comparison, and final interpretation — a structure designed to ensure findings could be mapped back to both the academic literature and the original research question.





  Skills developed
  
    
      Critical reading
      Synthesising and evaluating peer-reviewed empirical studies across different methodological approaches
    
    
      Research design
      Constructing a qualitative interview methodology with participant criteria, question design, and analysis plan
    
    
      Thematic analysis
      Applying a structured coding framework to qualitative data to surface patterns across respondents
    
    
      Academic writing
      Communicating complex research design decisions clearly within a 1,169-word constraint
    
  





  Reflection
  This module pushed me to engage with academic sources differently from any other assignment I had done. Rather than simply summarising what studies found, the critical thinking framework required me to interrogate why they found it, what methodological assumptions underpinned their conclusions, and what gaps they left open. Reading Gajendran and Harrison's meta-analysis alongside the Galanti et al. pandemic-era study made clear how significantly context shapes findings — the same variable, autonomy, functions very differently when remote work is chosen versus imposed.
  Designing the interview methodology was the most practically useful part. Mapping the literature themes onto specific interview questions and then planning how those answers would be coded made the connection between theory and evidence feel concrete rather than abstract. That process — from question to data to analysis to conclusion — is something I have applied to every research task since.

About the project
BAA1028 Workflow & Data Management is the module that asks students to demonstrate, in a single deliverable, how reproducible workflows, version control discipline and structured data management are actually applied in practice. The deliverable is this ePortfolio: a publicly hosted website built from raw markup and styling rather than a CMS, version-controlled in Git, deployed automatically to GitHub Pages, and structured around data files that the page builds itself reads at render time.
I came into this module with prior experience building websites in WordPress and Elementor Pro for freelance clients. WordPress hides almost everything that this module is about: there is no Git history, no build pipeline, no concept of structured frontmatter, no separation between content and presentation. Switching to Quarto for this project meant doing all of those things explicitly, in code, for the first time. That gap between “I can build a website” and “I can build a reproducible web project” is precisely what BAA1028 is about, and it is what this page sets out to demonstrate.






NoteWhy this page is different from the other project pages



Every other page in this portfolio describes work that happened elsewhere and reproduces selected exhibits as Plotly charts. This page is meta: the project being described is the website you are reading, and the charts below analyse the actual repository at github.com/alekslupa/alekslupa.github.io. The data is generated by a small Python script (scripts/generate_repo_stats.py) that walks the Git history and the file tree, writes results to four CSV files in data/, and the page reads those CSVs at render time. That separation between data generation and presentation is itself a workflow choice the module is graded on.

A note about what this chart does and does not show. It shows the size of the file over time, not the quality of the code in it. SCSS that is large and well-organised is fine; SCSS that is large and chaotic is not. The qualitative judgement requires reading the file. The quantitative trend gives an accurate impression of effort distribution: the styling work accumulated over many short sessions rather than landing in one or two giant commits at the end.

title: ePortfolio (this website)
text:
Reflection
This was the project that most directly demonstrated the gap between “I can build a website” and “I can build a reproducible web project”. Coming from a WordPress freelance background, I underestimated how much of the cognitive load of web development WordPress hides. Quarto, Git and GitHub Pages each force decisions that WordPress makes invisibly. None of those decisions are individually difficult, but they all have to be made explicitly, in code, and they all have downstream consequences. Choosing output-dir: docs is a one-line decision that determines what the deploy URL serves. Choosing to centralise styling in a single SCSS file means the visual language is consistent but also means the file becomes a bottleneck. Choosing YAML frontmatter as the project metadata format means listing pages are automatic but also means every project must conform to the schema.
The decision I am proudest of is the one that produced this page. Every other project page in the portfolio describes work that happened elsewhere and reproduces selected exhibits as Plotly charts. For the ePortfolio page itself, that approach would have been circular: the project being described is the website hosting the description. Instead, the page reads real data from the actual repository and analyses itself. The CSV-generation script (scripts/generate_repo_stats.py) walks the Git history and the file tree once, writes its outputs to data/, and the page reads from those CSVs at render time. The separation between data generation and presentation is itself the workflow pattern the module is teaching, and applying it to the page that describes the module’s deliverable felt like the right way to demonstrate understanding rather than just describing it.
The honest limitation is that the workflow shown on this page is overkill for a single-author static site. A team-of-one editor running one repo with one deployment target does not strictly need a separate data generation script, an explicit pipeline diagram, or a documented information architecture. The reason to do all of those things anyway is that they are the same patterns that scale to projects where the overkill becomes underkill quickly. Treating a small project with the workflow discipline of a large one is cheap; the inverse is expensive. That generalisation is what I want to take out of this module into whatever team-based analytics work I end up doing after graduation.
A second honest note: this is the first project I have built without any visual builder in the loop. The quality of the result is genuinely the result of code I wrote myself, with the help of AI tools (Claude, Gemini, Grammarly) for structural suggestions, debugging and proofreading. Every architectural decision is mine; every line of SCSS is either written or directly reviewed by me; every Plotly chart on this page is generated from a real CSV produced by my own script.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
About the research
This was my final research paper for the BAA1027 Machine Learning module, supervised by Dr Michael Farayola. Unlike my group projects, this was a solo piece of work from dataset selection through to final submission. The dataset is the Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention collection published by Sakar et al. (2019) and distributed through the UCI Machine Learning Repository: 12,330 online sessions described by 17 features and a binary Revenue target, with a moderate 15.5% positive class imbalance.
The research question was whether a standard comparative classifier pipeline could be meaningfully extended by three additions: K-means cluster labels injected as an engineered feature, a soft voting ensemble, and cost-sensitive threshold optimisation parameterised from published e-commerce economics. The empirical answer, reported honestly including the two innovations that did not work, produced a more interesting finding than if everything had worked: the decision rule matters more than the classifier.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The sections below reproduce the core findings of the research paper as executable Python with Plotly. The original notebook used matplotlib and seaborn in Google Colab; this page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as interactive charts for the portfolio. Click the </> Code button at the top to toggle all source code, or unfold any single chunk to inspect it. All numerical results originate from the executed notebook submitted for assessment.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
1. Classifier benchmark
Five classifiers were tuned via GridSearchCV with 5-fold stratified cross-validation, scoring on F1 rather than accuracy to reflect the class imbalance. XGBoost recorded the highest F1 (66.73%) and PR-AUC (74.53%), narrowly ahead of Random Forest. SVM and Logistic Regression lagged materially, the former on recall, the latter because a linear decision surface cannot model the non-linear PageValues saturation effect.


Code
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

results = pd.DataFrame({
    "Model":        ["Logistic Regression", "SVM (RBF)", "Random Forest", "XGBoost", "Voting Classifier"],
    "Precision":    [76.70, 68.86, 76.80, 73.12, 77.64],
    "Recall":       [37.41, 34.79, 52.10, 61.36, 44.93],
    "F1":           [50.29, 46.23, 62.08, 66.73, 56.92],
    "PR-AUC":       [63.68, 56.30, 73.06, 74.53, 71.77],
})

results = results.sort_values("F1", ascending=True)

fig = go.Figure()

metrics = {
    "Precision": "#4a90a4",
    "Recall":    "#d4a017",
    "F1":        "#1e7e34",
    "PR-AUC":    "#6a1b9a",
}

for metric, colour in metrics.items():
    fig.add_trace(go.Bar(
        y=results["Model"], x=results[metric],
        name=metric, orientation="h",
        marker=dict(color=colour),
        text=[f"{v:.1f}%" for v in results[metric]],
        textposition="outside",
        textfont=dict(size=11),
    ))

fig.update_layout(
    barmode="group",
    height=500,
    margin=dict(l=20, r=60, t=20, b=30),
    paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    plot_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)",
    font=dict(family="Inter, sans-serif", color="#1a1a1a"),
    xaxis=dict(range=[0, 95], showgrid=True, gridcolor="#eee", ticksuffix="%"),
    yaxis=dict(showgrid=False),
    legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.02, x=0),
)
fig.show()




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Classification metrics across the five tuned models. XGBoost wins on F1 and PR-AUC; the Voting Classifier wins on precision but loses recall, producing a lower F1 than XGBoost alone.




The Voting Classifier illustrates a counterintuitive result: it aggregates the four base learners via soft probability voting and achieves the highest precision of any model (77.64%), but it loses recall relative to XGBoost alone (44.93% vs 61.36%). The net effect is an F1 of 56.92%, ten points below XGBoost. Cornelio et al. (2021) show that voting ensembles produce marginal gains only when base learners have complementary failure modes. On this dataset they do not, so the ensemble is reported as a negative result rather than buried in the appendix.

3. The cost-sensitive threshold innovation
This is the paper’s central methodological contribution and its strongest empirical result. The default 0.5 classification threshold presumes symmetric misclassification costs, which is rarely appropriate in e-commerce. I derived a cost ratio from two published benchmarks: Littledata (2025) reports USD 92 average revenue per Shopify customer; WordStream (2025) reports USD 19.68 average Facebook Ads cost per acquisition. The ratio of 4.67 was rounded up to 5 to reflect a deliberate preference toward minority-class recall, then stress-tested across the 3:1 to 7:1 range.

Two results emerge from the sensitivity analysis. First, the optimal threshold is stable at 0.16 across ratios 3:1 through 6:1, shifting only modestly to 0.11 at 7:1. The threshold optimisation is robust to moderate misspecification of the cost ratio, which matters because the Littledata and WordStream benchmarks are US-based while the dataset is of unknown geography. Second, the cost reduction scales monotonically from 16.5% at the most conservative ratio to 41.9% at the most aggressive. Even at 3:1 the adjustment delivers double-digit savings.

import plotly.graph_objects as go

# Illustrative curve reconstructed from the paper's cost function
# Total cost = 5 * FN + 1 * FP under the 5:1 cost ratio

# Smooth U-shape with minimum around 0.16, calibrated to paper figures
# Default (0.5) cost = 1234, optimum (0.16) cost = 825

    base = 825 + 3200 * (t - 0.16) ** 2
    if t < 0.16:

    return base

4. What the threshold shift actually does
The cost reduction on its own is a summary statistic. The confusion-matrix shift underneath it shows the operational trade-off: at the optimal threshold the model catches far more positive cases but at the price of more false alarms. This is the right trade-off for an e-commerce retargeting use case where the cost of missing a potential converter (lost revenue) substantially exceeds the cost of showing an advert to a non-converter.

The key cell is the false-negative count. At the default threshold, 221 genuine buyers were classified as non-buyers, representing either missed retargeting opportunities or under-prioritised sessions in a live recommendation system. At the optimal threshold that figure drops to 82, recovering 139 previously misclassified converters. The cost of doing so is 286 additional false positives, but under the 5:1 cost ratio this is a favourable trade by design.

Limitations acknowledged in the paper






WarningFour limitations worth flagging




Single platform, single time window. The dataset reflects one e-commerce platform and a twelve-month collection window, which constrains generalisability.
Geographical mismatch on the cost ratio. The Littledata and WordStream benchmarks are US-based, while the dataset geography is unknown. The sensitivity analysis in Section 3 directly mitigates this concern by showing threshold stability across 3:1 to 7:1.
Single stratified split. Evaluation relies on one train/test partition, leaving metrics subject to sampling variance. k-fold test evaluation would tighten confidence intervals.
Scaler fitted on full dataset. The MinMaxScaler was applied to the full frame before the train/test split rather than fitted on the training partition only. The deterministic bounded nature of Min-Max scaling makes material impact unlikely, but the pattern should be corrected in production.

title: Online Shoppers Purchasing Intention
text:
Reflection
This was the most technically demanding piece of work of my degree. The core lesson was methodological rather than technical. Going into the project I expected the interesting finding to be which classifier won. What actually emerged was that the classifier choice mattered much less than the decision rule applied on top of it. The 33.1% cost reduction from the threshold shift is larger than the F1 gap between any two classifiers in the baseline comparison, which is a result I did not anticipate and which changed how I think about applied machine learning.
Reporting the two negative results honestly was a deliberate choice and the one that took most intellectual adjustment. K-means cluster injection and the soft voting ensemble were both methodologically defensible ideas when I designed them. Neither worked. The temptation to either bury them in the appendix or find a metric that made them look marginally favourable was real. Instead I kept them in the main narrative with an explicit framing as negative results and a reasoned explanation of why they failed (the tree ensembles had already extracted the available signal from the raw features, and the base learners lacked the complementary failure modes that voting ensembles depend on). Reading the resulting paper back, the negative results strengthen rather than weaken the overall argument, because they locate the positive result (cost-sensitive thresholding) more precisely in methodological space.
The broader takeaway I carried out of the module is that machine learning as a discipline is closer to applied statistics with a business objective than to computer science with a model zoo. The classifier is the smaller part of the problem. The decision rule, the evaluation design, the limitation audit and the feature interpretability are the parts that determine whether the model is useful or misleading. This is the lens I intend to apply in business analyst roles where similar risks apply: accuracy-optimising a model against a dataset that is not the real production distribution is the easiest way to produce an impressive-looking artefact that fails in deployment.

About the project
Our group of six acted as a consulting firm, A & A Consultancy, tasked with producing a full strategic review of Superdry, the British apparel brand that rose to become a FTSE-listed retailer and then collapsed into retrenchment and delisting. The report examined how the brand captured value in its early years, why it declined through overexpansion and brand dilution, and what strategic interventions could restore its competitive position.
The analysis followed a structured consulting process of Orientation, Diagnostics, Intervention, Evaluation, applying frameworks including PESTEL, Porter’s Five Forces, SWOT, RBV/VRIO, the Strategy Diamond and the ERRC Grid. As Associate Director I led analysis and synthesis work particularly across the Diagnostics and Evaluation stages, with input from the team across every section. The group built the underlying insights; this page rebuilds the key visual artefacts as interactive Plotly and Mermaid renders for the portfolio.






NoteWhat’s on this page



The visualisations below reproduce the core strategic artefacts from the Group BS1 Superdry report. Financial data comes from Superdry’s publicly reported annual accounts (FY2014 to FY2024); the framework scoring reflects our group’s consensus diagnostic rather than external research. The original report used static exhibits; this page rebuilds the same underlying analysis as executable Python with Plotly, plus Mermaid for the conceptual diagrams, as a portfolio extension.

The implication is blunt: Superdry cannot win by trying to out-compete Shein on price or Nike on scale. A mid-market undifferentiated player in this industry structure has no natural profit pool. Either re-establish meaningful differentiation or continue margin compression indefinitely.

text:
3. The Value Stick, shortened
The Value Stick concept frames strategic value capture as the vertical distance between a customer’s willingness to pay (WTP) at the top and the firm’s cost at the bottom, with price sitting in between. A healthy brand runs a long stick: high WTP, controlled costs, room for both consumer surplus and firm margin.
Superdry’s decline can be read cleanly on this frame. Between 2012 and 2023, WTP compressed (the brand lost its premium cachet), costs rose (through discounting, logistics complexity and wholesale dilution), and the stick shortened dramatically.

This is the vicious cycle described in the report’s Diagnostics section: low-margin, volume-based economic logic that destroys brand value and profitability simultaneously.

4. SWOT synthesis
The internal analysis surfaced a stark gap between genuine residual strengths (brand recognition, design archive, founder-led creative direction) and acute weaknesses (brand dilution, weak digital, high-cost legacy model, debt overhang). Viewed as a diagnostic rather than an inventory, the SWOT makes two points clear. First, the strengths are heritage assets: real but finite, and they depreciate fast without investment. Second, the weaknesses and threats reinforce each other (perpetual discounting plus cost-of-living pressure plus weak digital plus fierce competition form a trap). Any renewal strategy has to break that reinforcing loop.

text:
Reflection
This was my first experience working in a consulting format with a formally defined team structure and a real business case. The most valuable lesson was learning how frameworks that look mechanical on the page (PESTEL, Five Forces, Strategy Diamond) function very differently when applied to an actual declining company with incomplete information. The Strategy Diamond in particular was initially treated by the group as a five-box summary exercise and only became useful when we started arguing about which of the five elements was the hinge. That debate (which we eventually resolved on the Economic Logic element) was the point at which our analysis graduated from description into diagnosis.
The group dynamics were the other major learning. We hit a rough patch around the in-module presentation, where last-minute slide changes combined with IT issues produced a coordination failure that was uncomfortable at the time. Working through it afterwards, with a combination of honest conversation and shared resolve to make the report itself a strong piece of work, taught me more about managing team pressure than the frameworks themselves did. The skills matrix we drew up early in the project (a consulting tool I had not encountered before) turned out to be the single most useful organisational device we used, because it gave each member a defensible domain and reduced duplication.
Reproducing the analytical exhibits as interactive Python and Mermaid renders for this portfolio was a separate exercise from the module itself. The original report used static diagrams embedded in a designed PDF. Rebuilding them forced me to re-examine whether each framework actually added unique insight, or whether some were decorative rather than diagnostic. The Porter’s Five Forces radar and the Value Stick are, on reflection, the two frameworks that pulled the most analytical weight in the final argument. The others supported that argument rather than producing it independently.
Strategy as a discipline is less about running more frameworks and more about choosing the two or three that matter for the specific question, then applying them rigorously enough to produce a decision. That was the takeaway I carried out of the module, and it is the lens I intend to apply to business analytics roles where the risk is usually the same: too many dashboards, not enough diagnosis.
